pages.text: Noura had always been the weather expert in her family. While her cousins checked football scores, she checked wind speeds and cloud maps on her phone. So when her grandfather invited everyone to his farm near the mountains for the weekend, she was the first to look at the forecast. "Clear skies all day," she announced. "Perfect for a picnic in the wadi."

The wadi was a wide, dry valley behind the farm, full of smooth stones and soft sand. Her younger brother Saad and their cousins Hamad and Lulwa raced ahead, laughing and kicking up dust. Grandfather walked slowly behind them with his stick, while Mother and Aunt Huda spread a carpet under an acacia tree. Above them, the sky was a perfect, burning blue.

After lunch, Noura noticed something strange. Far away, over the mountains, dark clouds had gathered, tall and grey like towers. A low rumble of thunder rolled across the valley, so quiet that nobody else seemed to hear it. She opened her weather app again, and this time a yellow warning was flashing: heavy rain in the highlands.

"Grandfather, it's raining in the mountains," she said. He was already looking at the horizon, and his face had become serious. "When I was a boy, we had a saying," he replied. "The wadi remembers every drop that falls on the mountains, and sooner or later it brings them home." Noura felt a cold shiver, even though the air was hot.

She understood immediately. All that rain would run down the slopes and into the valley, straight towards them. "Everyone, we need to move to higher ground now!" she shouted. Hamad rolled his eyes. "You're worrying about nothing. There isn't a single cloud above us!"

Then Lulwa pointed at the ground. A thin line of brown water was sliding between the stones, quietly, like a snake. A strange smell of wet earth filled the air, and a deep roar was growing louder somewhere up the valley. Nobody argued after that.

They grabbed the carpet and the baskets and hurried up the rocky bank, with Saad holding Grandfather's arm. They had only just reached the top when the flood arrived. A wall of muddy water rushed through the wadi, carrying branches, stones and even their forgotten football. The acacia tree where they had been sitting minutes before was now standing in a fast, wild river.

For a long time, nobody spoke, and then Hamad turned to Noura. "I should have listened to you," he said quietly. Grandfather put his hand on her shoulder and smiled. "Your phone and my old saying told the same story," he said, "and a wise person listens to both." The next morning, the wadi was dry again, but Noura knew she would never trust a blue sky so easily.

pages.text: Every afternoon, Faisal walked home through the narrow streets of Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. He always stopped under the same tall house, with its coral-stone walls and dark wooden windows called rawasheen. One window had a hole where a carved panel had once been, like a missing tooth in a smile. "Your great-grandfather made that window," his grandfather had told him, "but the last piece was broken long before you were born."

At school, Mr. Khalid announced a competition: the winning student would design a large mural for the entrance of the new community centre. "Show us something that belongs to this city," he said. Faisal's best friend, Omar, was already sketching camels and palm trees, but Faisal just stared at his empty page. He had never been good at drawing, and his camels looked like potatoes with legs.

That evening, Faisal sat with his grandfather on the roof and admitted that he had no ideas at all. Grandfather went inside and came back with an old notebook. Inside there were no pictures, only circles, lines and stars, all made with a compass and a ruler. "Every pattern begins with one circle," he said. "If you understand the circle, you can build anything."

For two weeks, Faisal filled page after page with eight-pointed stars that joined together like a chain. His final design was a huge wall of stars inspired by the old window, with one shape in the centre left empty. The night before the deadline, he left it on the kitchen table. In the morning, he found his little brother Saud beside it, holding an empty cup of karak tea, and the paper had soaked up every drop.

"I'm sorry! I was only looking at it," Saud cried. Faisal wanted to shout, but when he saw the tears in his brother's eyes, he took a deep breath instead. There were only three hours left before he had to hand in his design. "Then you can help me," he said, grabbing a new sheet, his compass and his ruler. "Hold the paper flat and don't let it move."

At first his hands were shaking, and his first circle came out wrong. Then he remembered Grandfather's words and started again, slowly. Circle by circle, line by line, the stars returned, as if they had been waiting inside his head all along. This time he noticed something he had missed before: the empty shape in the centre was exactly the size of the missing panel in the old window. He finished in the nick of time and ran to school with ink all over his fingers.

A week later, Mr. Khalid read out the winner's name, and Faisal was so surprised that Omar had to push him out of his chair. "The judges loved the way your design connects the past and the present," Mr. Khalid said. "But they want to know why there's an empty space in the middle." Faisal smiled. "Because some pieces of our city are still missing," he replied, "and someone has to finish them."

That spring, the whole class helped to paint the mural, but the best moment came afterwards. With the owner's permission, Faisal and his grandfather carved a small wooden panel in the same star pattern and fitted it into the old window in Al-Balad. Saud insisted on holding the screws, and nobody argued. Under the evening sun, the window looked complete for the first time in fifty years, like a smile with no missing teeth.

pages.text: Every summer, Noura spent a week at her grandmother's old house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. The house had tall wooden windows, narrow stairs and a cool room full of things that nobody used any more. On a high shelf in that room stood an hourglass made of dark wood and glass. "Look at it as much as you like," her grandmother always said, "but never turn it over."

One hot afternoon, while her grandmother was resting, Noura climbed onto a chair to take a closer look. The sand inside wasn't yellow but silver, and it seemed to shine on its own. She told herself that she would only hold it for a moment, but as she lifted it, it slipped in her hands and turned upside down. The room began to spin, and the silver sand started to fall.

When Noura opened her eyes, she was standing in the same street, but everything had changed. The parked cars and air conditioners had disappeared, and the street was crowded with carts, donkeys and men selling dates and fabric. An old song was playing on a radio in a shop, and a calendar on the wall said 1965. With her heart beating fast, Noura realised that she had travelled back almost sixty years.

Near an old well, a girl of about her age was searching the ground, close to tears. "My father trusted me with the key to his shop, and I've lost it," she explained. "If I don't find it before sunset, he won't be able to lock the door tonight." Noura could feel the hourglass in her pocket and guessed she didn't have long, but she couldn't just walk away. "Don't worry," she said with a smile. "Two pairs of eyes are better than one."

Together they retraced the girl's steps through the market, checking under baskets and between the stones. "Did you stop anywhere on the way?" Noura asked, and the girl remembered that she had bent down to drink from a water jar outside the mosque. Sure enough, a small brass key was lying in the shadow beside it. The girl, whose name was Hessa, laughed with relief and hugged her new friend.

Then Hessa noticed the phone in Noura's hand. "What is that strange glass box?" she asked, her eyes wide with wonder. Noura showed her a photo of modern Jeddah, with its towers shining by the sea, but before she could explain, she saw that only a few grains of sand were left. Feeling dizzy, she put the phone down on the edge of the well to hold the hourglass with both hands, and the whole world disappeared.

Noura woke up on the floor of the cool room, with the hourglass lying beside her. Her heart sank when she checked her pocket, because her phone was gone. She hurried downstairs, ready to apologise, but her grandmother was already waiting for her with a small tin box and a gentle smile. "I've been keeping this for you for a very long time," she said.

Inside the box was Noura's phone, old and dusty, its battery long dead. Next to it lay a piece of paper, yellow with age, covered in a child's careful handwriting: "For the girl who helped me find my father's key. I promise to keep your glass box safe until you come back." At the bottom was a name, Hessa, and Noura looked up at her grandmother in amazement. "Some things only happen at the right time," her grandmother said softly, "and today, at last, was the right time."

pages.text: Every morning before school, Reem and her younger brother Faisal walked along the muddy shore near their grandfather's house in Jazan. For two weeks, they had been looking after forty tiny mangrove seedlings, which their science class had planted in the shallow water. Their teacher, Ms. Hanan, had explained that mangrove forests protect the coast from storms and give young fish a safe place to grow. Reem was determined to keep every single plant alive.

But on Thursday morning, Faisal stopped suddenly and pointed. "Reem, look! Six of them are gone!" Where the seedlings had stood the day before, there were only small holes in the mud. Reem felt her heart sink. "Someone is stealing them," she said, "and we're going to get to the bottom of this."

That evening, they told their grandfather, who had been a fisherman for forty years. He listened carefully while he drank his tea. "Before you accuse anyone, you need evidence," he said. "Watch the shore at low tide, when the water goes out. The sea always tells its secrets then." Faisal suddenly had an idea: they could hide his old phone in a tree and record a video.

The next afternoon, they fixed the phone to a low branch and pointed it at the seedlings. After school the following day, they checked the video, full of excitement. For a long time, nothing happened except the tide slowly going out. Then, just after sunset, something moved across the mud. Faisal leaned closer to the screen. "It's not a person at all," he whispered.

Dozens of small red crabs were climbing out of holes in the mud. With their claws, they grabbed the soft young leaves and pulled the seedlings down into their burrows. Reem couldn't help laughing, even though she was disappointed. "So our thieves have eight legs!" Grandfather smiled. "Crabs are part of the mangrove forest too," he said. "Big trees can survive them, but baby plants need protection."

But how could they protect the seedlings? Then Reem remembered the pile of plastic bottles she had collected during a beach clean-up the month before. "What if we cut the bottles and put one around each seedling, like a wall?" she asked. "Rubbish that saves a forest? That's genius!" Faisal said. All weekend, they washed and cut the bottles, then pushed them into the mud, leaving the tops open for sunlight and air.

A week later, they checked the shore again, and they were over the moon. Every protected seedling was still standing, and some even had new green leaves. When Ms. Hanan came to see, she was so impressed that she asked them to present their idea to the whole school. Soon, students were bringing bottles from home, and the project grew from forty plants to more than three hundred.

Months later, when the young trees were strong enough, the bottles were removed and recycled, so no plastic was left on the shore. One evening, Reem and Faisal sat with their grandfather and watched the sun set over their small green forest. Tiny fish were swimming between the roots. "You solved the mystery," Grandfather said, "but you also made peace with the crabs." Reem smiled, because she had learned that protecting nature doesn't mean fighting it, but understanding it.

pages.text: Every morning before school, Omar helped his grandfather at the small bakery in the old part of Taif. He loved the smell of fresh bread and the heavy sound of the oven door closing. But recently, something strange had been happening. Each morning, one loaf disappeared from the shelf by the back door, and in its place there was a tiny wooden bird.

"Someone is stealing from us, Jiddo," Omar said, holding up the seventh bird. His grandfather simply smiled and put it on the high shelf next to the others. "Stealing? A thief doesn't leave presents," he replied. Omar wasn't convinced, so he decided to find out the truth himself.

The next morning, he arrived an hour early and hid behind the flour sacks. Just as the sky was turning pink, the back door opened quietly. A thin boy about his own age stepped inside, took a loaf, and carefully placed a small carved falcon on the shelf. Omar jumped out. "Caught you red-handed!" he shouted.

The boy froze, and the bread almost fell from his hands. "I'm not a thief," he said in a shaking voice. "My name is Sami. We moved here three months ago, and my father hasn't been able to work since his accident." He looked down at the floor. "I can't pay with money, so I pay with what I make."

Before Omar could answer, his grandfather appeared in the doorway. "Good morning, Sami," he said warmly, as if he had been expecting him. Omar stared at him. "You knew all along?" His grandfather nodded and explained that he had left that loaf by the back door on purpose every single day.

Later, while Sami ate breakfast with them, Grandfather told a story Omar had never heard before. "When I was a boy, my family had very little," he said. "A baker in Makkah gave us bread every morning, and he never once made me feel ashamed. Real kindness doesn't only fill someone's stomach, Omar. It also protects their pride."

Omar felt his face go hot as he remembered shouting at Sami. "I'm sorry," he said. "I should have asked before I accused you." Then he looked up at the shelf of wooden birds, and an idea came to him. "Sami, these are amazing. People would buy them, I'm sure of it."

By the end of the month, the shelf above the counter had become the most popular corner of the bakery. Customers came for bread but left with falcons, doves and hoopoes, and Sami's family no longer had to worry about the rent. Every morning, Omar still put one loaf by the back door, just in case someone else needed it. And next to it, he left a small note: "Take what you need. No questions asked."

dialogue.t: So, how much time do you spend on your phone these days?
Honestly, I've been spending about four hours a day on my phone lately, mostly watching videos.
Wow, that's quite a lot! I tend to check my messages whenever I feel bored.
Me too. Compared to last year, I use social media much more, but I read much less.
Maybe we should set a limit together. What about two hours on school days?
That sounds fair. I could also turn off notifications while I'm doing homework.
Great idea. And how about no phones at dinner?

grammar.title: Present Perfect Continuous for Recent Habits

examples: I've been spending too much time on games lately.
She's been using a new study app for two weeks.
We've been watching fewer videos since we set a limit.

dialogue.t: I think video games are a waste of time. What do you think?
I disagree. One advantage of gaming is that it helps you solve problems quickly.
I see your point, but many teenagers play for hours and forget their homework.
That's true. On the other hand, team games teach you how to work with other people.
Maybe, but sitting in front of a screen all day isn't healthy.
I see your point, but that's why we should play in moderation, not stop completely.
OK, I agree with that. Games can be fun if we don't overdo it.

grammar.title: Contrasting Ideas Politely
grammar.ar: نستخدم On the other hand في بداية جملة جديدة لعرض فكرة معاكسة، وتأتي بعدها فاصلة. أما I see your point, but فنستخدمها لإظهار احترامنا لرأي الآخر قبل أن نعارضه بلطف. وبعد One advantage of نستخدم اسمًا أو فعلًا بصيغة ing، مثل: One advantage of playing games is that...

dialogue.t: I just got a message saying my game account will be closed unless I send my password.
That sounds suspicious. If I were you, I'd ignore it and not reply.
But what if it's real? I don't want to lose my account.
Real companies never ask for that. You should never share your password because someone could steal your account.
OK. Should I just delete the message?
It's a good idea to take a screenshot before you delete it. Then block the sender and report it.
Thanks! I'll also tell my parents about it.
Good thinking. And if I were you, I'd change your password just to be safe.

Definitely a language-learning app. What I like most about it is the daily challenges.
Sounds fun! Is it easy to use?

dialogue.t: Which invention do you think changed everyday life the most?
I'd say the telephone. It was invented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876.
Interesting! How did people communicate before that?
Before the telephone existed, people used to send letters, and they took weeks to arrive.
Wow, that's slow! Can you imagine life without phones today?
Not really. Without phones, we wouldn't be able to call our families quickly in an emergency.
True. And smartphones have replaced cameras, maps, and even alarm clocks!
Exactly. One small device does everything now.

grammar.title: Past Passive and Used To
grammar.ar: نستخدم المبني للمجهول في الماضي (was/were + التصريف الثالث للفعل) عندما يكون الاختراع نفسه أهم من الشخص الذي صنعه، ونذكر الفاعل بعد by والسنة بعد in. ونستخدم used to + الفعل في المصدر للحديث عن عادات كانت في الماضي ولم تعد موجودة الآن. انتبه: نقول was invented وليس invented وحدها عندما يكون الاختراع هو الفاعل في الجملة.

dialogue.t: What do you think schools will be like in 2040?
By 2040, I think we'll have virtual reality lessons. We could explore space in science class!
That sounds amazing. Do you think robots will replace teachers?
No, it's unlikely that robots will replace teachers completely. Students still need real people.
I agree. What about our homes?

Sounds fair. But who's going to measure the plants every day?
We could take turns. You do Mondays and Wednesdays, and I'll do the other days.
OK. Let's make sure we finish all the measurements by next Thursday.
Good idea. And let's make sure we practise the presentation by the 18th, so we have time to fix any problems.
Deal. I'll send us both a reminder so we stay on schedule.

dialogue.t: Hey Layla, are you upset with me? You didn't reply to my messages.
Well, yes. You told the teacher I didn't do my part of the project.
Oh no! I think you might have misunderstood what I said. I told her your part wasn't finished yet, not that you didn't do it.
Really? From my point of view, it sounded like you were blaming me.
I'm really sorry. I didn't mean to make you look bad. I just wanted to explain why we needed more time.
OK, I understand now. And I didn't mean to ignore you. I was just angry.
Let's sort it out. Next time, we can talk to the teacher together.
That's a good idea. Thanks for explaining.

dialogue.t: You look tired, Yousef. Are you OK?
Not really. I'm so stressed out about the final exams. I can't concentrate on anything.
Have you tried making a revision timetable? It shows you exactly what to study each day.
No, I haven't. I usually just study whatever I find first.
It might help if you took short breaks every hour, too. Your brain needs some rest.
That makes sense. What would you do if you had three exams in two days?
I'd start with the hardest subject, and I'd make sure I got enough sleep before each exam.
Thanks, that's really helpful. I'll try it tonight.

grammar.title: Reported speech: statements, questions and instructions
grammar.ar: عندما ننقل كلام شخص آخر نستخدم said that، وعادةً نرجع زمن الفعل خطوة إلى الماضي: is تصبح was، و can تصبح could، و will تصبح would. ولنقل سؤال جوابه نعم أو لا نستخدم asked (me) if + جملة عادية بدون do/does وبترتيب الخبر، وليس بترتيب السؤال. ولنقل الأوامر نستخدم told + الشخص + to + الفعل. انتبه: told يحتاج دائمًا إلى شخص بعده (told us)، أما said فلا.
examples: He said that the bus would leave at seven.

dialogue.t: You look worried, Karim. What's wrong?
I'm torn between the football team and the coding club. They both meet on Tuesdays.
That's a tough one. Have you thought about the pros and cons?
Yes. On the one hand, I love football and all my friends are on the team. On the other hand, coding could really help me in the future.
Could you do one this term and the other one next term?
Maybe. I've been weighing it up all week, but it's still hard to make up my mind.
So, what did you choose in the end?
In the end, I decided to join the coding club because the football season finishes in March, and I can join the team again next year.

grammar.title: Talking about choices and decisions
grammar.ar: نستخدم I'm torn between X and Y لنقول إننا محتارون بين خيارين، وبعدها اسم أو فعل بـ ing. ونستخدم On the one hand ... On the other hand ... لعرض جانبين مختلفين من الموضوع. ولنقول ما اخترناه في النهاية نستخدم In the end, I decided to + الفعل الأساسي + because + السبب. انتبه: نقول decided to join وليس decided join أو decided for join.
examples: I'm torn between learning Spanish and learning French.

dialogue.t: Looking back, do you have any regrets from this school year?
Yes, one big one. I left my history project until the last minute, and I got a really bad mark.
Oh no. What happened?
I stayed up all night and made lots of silly mistakes. I wish I had started earlier.
Something similar happened to me with the science fair. If I had known how long it would take, I would have asked for help sooner.
So what lesson did you learn?
Next time, I'll make sure to plan everything on a calendar.
Good idea. Next time, I'll make sure to start on the same day I get the task.

grammar.title: Regrets: wish + past perfect and the third conditional
grammar.ar: للتعبير عن الندم على شيء حدث في الماضي نستخدم I wish I had + التصريف الثالث (مثل I wish I had studied). وللحديث عن ماضٍ لا يمكن تغييره نستخدم الشرط الثالث: If I had + التصريف الثالث، ثم I would have + التصريف الثالث. وللحديث عن خطة في المستقبل بعد تعلّم الدرس نستخدم Next time, I'll make sure to + الفعل الأساسي. انتبه: لا نستخدم would في الجزء الذي يبدأ بـ if.
examples: I wish I had listened to my teacher's advice.
If I had known about the test, I would have revised more.
Next time, I'll make sure to check the deadline.

words.ar: يحافظ على المياه / يرشّد استهلاك المياه
words.ex: We should all conserve water because it is very precious in our region.
Native trees like the ghaf tree need very little water to grow.
Many plants die during a long drought.
Our class made a plan to reduce waste in the school canteen.
The Saudi Green Initiative aims to plant billions of trees across the Kingdom.
Trees give shade and keep our streets cooler in summer.

dialogue.t: Have you read about the Saudi Green Initiative? It aims to plant ten billion trees across the Kingdom.
Yes! I think we ought to help in order to make our neighbourhood greener.
But trees need water, and water is precious here.
True. If everyone turned off the tap while brushing their teeth, we could save thousands of litres every day.
Good point. One thing our school could do is collect the water from the air conditioners and use it for the plants.
That's realistic! We ought to choose native trees in order to save even more water.
Let's suggest both ideas to our head teacher tomorrow.
Great. I'll write the proposal tonight.

grammar.title: Suggestions and purpose: ought to / in order to
grammar.ar: نستخدم ought to مع الفعل في صورته الأساسية لتقديم اقتراح أو نصيحة، ومعناها قريب من should أي «ينبغي». ونستخدم in order to مع الفعل في صورته الأساسية لبيان الهدف، بمعنى «لكي». انتبه: لا نضع to بعد should، أما ought فلا بد أن تتبعها to دائمًا.
examples: We ought to plant more trees in order to reduce the heat in our cities.
Families ought to fix leaking taps in order to save water.
Our school ought to start a recycling club in order to reduce waste.

words.ex: Saudi Arabia will host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
The new stadium will have seats for more than 40,000 fans.
Big sporting events can help tourism grow very quickly.
The country is improving its infrastructure, such as roads, airports and metro lines.
I'd love to volunteer at a big event and help visitors find their way.
The World Cup is a great opportunity to show our culture to the world.

dialogue.t: Saudi Arabia is hosting the World Cup in 2034! I'm really looking forward to watching a match in a real stadium.
Me too! It will give young players the chance to see world-class football up close.
And millions of fans are expected to visit the country.
That means more hotels and better transport. It will give local businesses the chance to grow.
Do you think it will change ordinary people's lives too?
I think so. More people are expected to start playing sport, and that's good for everyone's health.
By 2034, I'll be in my twenties. Maybe I'll work as a volunteer!
That would be amazing. I'm looking forward to volunteering too.

grammar.title: looking forward to + -ing / be expected to
grammar.ar: بعد عبارة looking forward to نستخدم الفعل مع ing أو اسمًا، لأن to هنا حرف جر وليست جزءًا من الفعل. لذلك نقول I'm looking forward to watching وليس to watch. أما be expected to فيليها الفعل في صورته الأساسية، ومعناها «من المتوقع أن».
examples: I'm really looking forward to meeting fans from all over the world.
The new metro is expected to open before the tournament.
We're looking forward to the opening ceremony.

words.ex: The headline sounded shocking, but the story was boring.

words.ar: على ما يبدو / حسب ما يُقال
words.ex: Apparently, the new park will open next month.
Fake news spreads very fast on social media.
Always check the story with a reliable source before you share it.
There's a rumour that our school trip is cancelled, but nobody knows for sure.
Journalists fact-check every story before they publish it.

dialogue.t: Did you hear that a camel in Riyadh learned to use a lift by itself?
Really? Where did you read that?
Apparently, it was on a website I found yesterday. There's even a video.
Hmm, that can't be true because camels are far too big for a normal lift.
You're right. And the website only had strange stories, no real news.
Then it must be fake. Real news usually appears on more than one reliable source.
OK, what about this one? Did you hear that scientists discovered a new kind of frog last year?
That must be true because scientists find new species every year. But let's fact-check it anyway.

grammar.title: Deduction: must / can't
grammar.ar: نستخدم must مع الفعل في صورته الأساسية عندما نكون متأكدين تقريبًا أن الشيء صحيح بناءً على دليل. ونستخدم can't عندما نكون متأكدين أنه مستحيل أو غير صحيح. انتبه: عكس must في الاستنتاج هو can't وليس mustn't، لأن mustn't تعني «ممنوع».
examples: That story must be real because it's on every news channel.
This photo can't be real because the shadows are wrong.
He must be tired; he has been travelling all day.

words.ex: My older sister is my role model because she works so hard.
I admire people who help others without expecting anything back.
She was determined to finish the race even though she was tired.
He overcame many difficulties to become a doctor.
You can achieve your goals if you never give up.
Even after winning the prize, he stayed humble and kind.

dialogue.t: Who inspires you the most?
Rayyanah Barnawi. She's someone who followed her dream and never gave up.
Isn't she the first Saudi woman to travel to space?
Yes, in 2023. She has achieved so much by studying science for many years and doing research.
That's impressive! What do you admire most about her?
What I admire most is the way she encourages young people to love science. What about you?
My grandfather. He's someone who always helps our neighbours. What I admire most is the way he stays patient with everyone.
He sounds like a great role model.

grammar.title: Describing people: who / by + -ing
grammar.ar: نستخدم who بعد كلمة تدل على شخص مثل someone أو a person لنضيف وصفًا له، ولا نكرر الضمير بعدها، فنقول someone who helps وليس someone who he helps. ونستخدم by مع الفعل المنتهي بـ ing لنشرح الطريقة التي حقق بها الشخص شيئًا، بمعنى «عن طريق».
examples: My teacher is someone who always believes in her students.
He became a champion by training every single day.
She has helped many families by starting a charity in her city.

words.ex: Good communication skills are important in almost every job.
A job outdoors would really suit someone who loves nature.
Many future jobs will involve working with artificial intelligence.
Engineers in renewable energy design solar and wind power projects.
You need to be creative to work as a game designer.
She wants a career in medicine because she loves helping people.

dialogue.t: Have you thought about what you want to do in the future?
I'm thinking of becoming a data scientist because I love maths and computers.
Cool. To do this job, you need to be patient and good at solving problems.
Exactly. What about you?
I'm not sure yet. I'd rather work outdoors than sit in an office all day.
Then maybe you could be a renewable energy engineer. Saudi Arabia is building huge solar farms.
That sounds interesting! But to do this job, you need to be good at physics.
Well, you'd rather study physics than work in an office, right?

grammar.title: Preferences: would rather ... than ...
grammar.ar: نستخدم would rather للتعبير عن تفضيل شيء على آخر، ويأتي بعدها الفعل في صورته الأساسية بدون to. نضع than قبل الخيار الثاني، ويكون الفعل بعدها أيضًا في صورته الأساسية. وفي الكلام نختصر I would إلى I'd.
examples: I'd rather design apps than repair cars.
She'd rather work in a team than work alone.
We'd rather study engineering than business.

words.ex: Start by introducing your topic clearly in one sentence.
My main point is that every student can help the environment.
Some jobs, for example drone pilots, didn't exist twenty years ago.
Look at your audience when you are speaking.
In your conclusion, repeat your most important idea.
At the end, summarise your talk in two or three sentences.

dialogue.t: Today I'd like to talk about how our school can save water.
First of all, we could fix all the leaking taps. One dripping tap can waste a lot of water every day.
Another point is that we could use water from the air conditioners for the school garden.
To sum up, small changes at school can make a big difference for our environment. Thank you for listening.
Thank you, that was very clear. Which idea do you think is the easiest to start with?
I think fixing the taps is the easiest, because it's quick and doesn't cost much.
Good answer. And how could students help?
Students could report leaking taps to the teachers and remind their friends to turn off the water.

grammar.title: Structuring a talk with linking phrases
grammar.ar: لكي يكون عرضك واضحًا، قسّمه إلى بداية ووسط ونهاية. نبدأ بعبارة Today I'd like to talk about لتقديم الموضوع، ثم نرتّب الأفكار بعبارات مثل First of all وAnother point is وFinally. وفي النهاية نستخدم To sum up لتلخيص الفكرة الرئيسية قبل شكر الجمهور.
examples: Today I'd like to talk about the jobs of the future.
First of all, technology is changing very fast. Another point is that new skills are needed.
To sum up, we need to keep learning to be ready for the future.

words.ex: Our budget for the weekend trip is 3,000 riyals.
We need to find accommodation close to the old town.
It's cheaper to book in advance, especially during the holidays.
The desert camp was comfortable and affordable.
We could rent a car at the airport and drive to Hegra.
The guided tour explained the history of the ancient tombs.

dialogue.t: We've got a free weekend next month. How about going to AlUla?
Great idea! But it's really far from Riyadh. Should we drive?
Wouldn't it be better to fly? Driving would take more than eleven hours.
True, but flights can be expensive. We could either fly and rent a car there, or drive and stop in Hail for a night.
Let's check our budget first. How about booking the flights in advance? They're usually more affordable.
Good thinking. For activities, we could either take a guided tour of Hegra or go hiking near Elephant Rock.
Why not both? Hegra in the morning and Elephant Rock at sunset.
Perfect! Let's look for accommodation tonight before everything gets booked.

grammar.title: Making and comparing suggestions
grammar.ar: نستخدم How about متبوعة بفعل ينتهي بـ ing- لنقترح فكرة، مثل: How about going…؟ ولا نقول How about go. ونستخدم Wouldn't it be better to متبوعة بالفعل في صورته الأساسية لنقترح خيارًا أفضل بأسلوب مهذب. أما either … or فنستخدمها لنعرض خيارين، ويأتي بعدهما نفس نوع الكلمة (فعل مع فعل، أو اسم مع اسم).
examples: How about staying in a desert camp instead of a hotel?
Wouldn't it be better to leave early in the morning?
We could either visit the old town or take a hot-air balloon ride.

words.ex: Kingdom Centre is one of the most famous landmarks in Riyadh.
The old town is a must-see for every visitor.
Kabsa is a traditional dish that most Saudi families love.
The market gets very crowded on Thursday evenings.
The National Museum is definitely worth visiting.
The view from the top of the tower is breathtaking.

dialogue.t: Hi! I've just arrived in Jeddah. What do you think I should see first?
You really have to see Al-Balad, the old town. It's famous for its old coral houses with wooden balconies.
That sounds amazing. When should I go there?
The best time to visit is in the evening because it's cooler and the streets are full of life.
Great. And what about food? I'd love to try something local.
You really have to try mutabbaq. It's a traditional dish, and the small restaurants in Al-Balad are famous for it.
Is there anywhere with a nice view of the sea?
Yes, the Corniche. The best time to go is at sunset because the sky and the fountain look breathtaking.

grammar.title: Giving strong recommendations
grammar.ar: نستخدم You really have to متبوعة بالفعل الأساسي لننصح شخصًا بشدة بشيء ما، وهنا لا تعني "إجبارًا" بل تعني "لا تفوّت هذا". ونستخدم It's famous for متبوعة باسم أو فعل ينتهي بـ ing- لنذكر سبب شهرة المكان. ولتحديد أفضل وقت نقول: The best time to visit is … because … ثم نذكر السبب في جملة كاملة.
examples: You really have to visit the Edge of the World near Riyadh.
Taif is famous for its roses and its cool weather.
The best time to visit is in winter because the weather is mild.

words.ex: Our flight to Dammam was delayed because of a sandstorm.
Please show your boarding pass at the gate.
We waited at baggage claim for almost an hour.
I almost missed my connecting flight in Dubai.
Write your phone number on the luggage tag.
You need to fill in a form to report a missing bag.

dialogue.t: Excuse me, could you tell me where the lost baggage desk is? My bag hasn't arrived yet.
You're in the right place. Can I see your boarding pass and luggage tag, please?
Here you are. My bag hasn't arrived yet. It's a large blue suitcase with black wheels and a red ribbon on the handle.
Thank you. It probably stayed in Dubai because your connecting flight was delayed. It should arrive tonight.
Would it be possible to send it to my hotel? I don't want to come back to the airport.
Of course. Please fill in this form with your hotel address and phone number.
Thanks. And could you tell me what time the next flight from Dubai lands?
At nine o'clock. We'll send you a message as soon as your bag is here.

grammar.title: Polite indirect questions
grammar.ar: عندما نبدأ السؤال بعبارة مهذبة مثل Could you tell me، يصبح ترتيب الكلمات بعد أداة السؤال مثل الجملة الخبرية: الفاعل ثم الفعل. فنقول: Could you tell me where the desk is? وليس where is the desk. ونستخدم Would it be possible to متبوعة بالفعل الأساسي لنطلب شيئًا بأدب شديد.
examples: Could you tell me why the flight is delayed?
Excuse me, could you tell me where gate 12 is?
Would it be possible to change my seat to a window seat?

words.ex: Our trip to Abha was the most memorable holiday I've had.
I was really impressed by the size of the old fort.
The mountain scenery in the south is beautiful.
We got lost in the old market, but it was fun.
I bought a small clay pot as a souvenir.
Have you ever travelled abroad with your family?

dialogue.t: Have you ever been to Abha?
Yes, I have! I went there when I was eleven, during the summer holidays.
What was it like?
Amazing. The thing that impressed me most was the cable car ride over the green mountains.
That sounds memorable. Did anything funny happen?
Yes, we got lost in the fog on the way to Al-Soudah! What about you? Have you ever been abroad?
Yes, I've been to Malaysia. I went there when I finished university.
Cool! What impressed you most?

grammar.title: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام (have/has + التصريف الثالث) لنسأل أو نتحدث عن التجارب في الحياة دون تحديد وقت، مثل: Have you ever been to…؟ وعندما نذكر وقتًا محددًا في الماضي مثل when I was ten أو last year نستخدم الماضي البسيط. لذلك نقول: I went there last year وليس I have been there last year.
examples: Have you ever been to AlUla?
I've visited Makkah three times.
I went to Egypt when I was nine, and I loved the pyramids.

words.ex: Saudi people are famous for their hospitality.
Serving Arabic coffee to guests is an old custom.
In Japan, people greet each other with a bow.
Please take off your shoes before you enter the majlis.
It can be impolite to refuse food when you are a guest.
In Germany, it's important to arrive on time.

dialogue.t: In Saudi Arabia, it's polite to serve guests Arabic coffee and dates, whereas in Britain people usually offer tea.
Interesting! Is there a special way to drink the coffee?
Yes. You're supposed to hold the cup in your right hand, and when you've had enough, you shake the cup gently.
That's a nice custom. In Japan, you're supposed to take off your shoes before you go into someone's home.
We do that too! In many countries, it's considered rude to refuse food when your host offers it.
True. And in Japan, people bow when they greet each other, whereas here people usually shake hands.
Is it considered rude to be late in Japan?
Very rude! You're supposed to arrive on time, or even a little early.

grammar.title: Talking about customs and rules
grammar.ar: نستخدم be supposed to متبوعة بالفعل الأساسي لنتحدث عمّا يتوقعه المجتمع من الناس، أي ما "ينبغي" فعله حسب العادات. ونستخدم It's considered rude/polite to لنقول إن الناس يرون تصرفًا ما غير مهذب أو مهذبًا. أما whereas فتعني "بينما" ونستخدمها للمقارنة بين بلدين أو عادتين مختلفتين.
examples: You're supposed to say 'Bismillah' before you start eating.
It's considered rude to point at people with your finger.
In Saudi Arabia, families eat dinner late, whereas in the UK people often eat at six.

words.ex: The train journey across Europe took two weeks.
Japan is my dream destination.
I'd love to explore the islands of the Red Sea.
Camping in the jungle would be a real adventure.

words.ar: تجربة لا تتكرر إلا مرة في العمر
words.ex: Seeing the Northern Lights is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
Kenya is famous for its amazing wildlife.

dialogue.t: If you could go anywhere in the world, where would you go?
If I could go anywhere, I'd travel to Norway. I've always wanted to see the Northern Lights because they look magical in photos.
Wow! What's the first thing you'd do there?
The first thing I'd do is take a boat trip along the fjords. Then I'd stay in a glass cabin and watch the sky at night.
That sounds like a once-in-a-lifetime journey.
What about you? What's your dream destination?
If I could go anywhere, I'd explore the Amazon rainforest. I've always wanted to see wildlife in nature, not in a zoo.
Wouldn't you be scared? Anyway, I guess that's part of the adventure!

grammar.title: The second conditional for imaginary situations
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية لنتحدث عن مواقف خيالية أو غير مرجحة الحدوث الآن. التركيب هو: If + فعل في الماضي البسيط، ثم would ('d) + الفعل الأساسي. لاحظ أن الفعل بعد If يكون في الماضي رغم أننا نتحدث عن الحاضر أو المستقبل، ولا نضع would بعد If مباشرة. ونستخدم I've always wanted to للتعبير عن أمنية قديمة ما زالت مستمرة.
examples: If I could go anywhere, I'd visit New Zealand.
If I had a lot of money, I'd travel around the world by ship.
I've always wanted to climb a mountain because I love a challenge.
